chapterTitle: Advanced Network Debugging and Troubleshooting with Ansible

screens.title: Advanced Network Debugging and Troubleshooting with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will see how Ansible becomes more than a configuration engine — it is a practical orchestration tool for diagnosing and resolving network issues on RHEL systems. You will learn how to collect comprehensive network facts automatically, run common diagnostic commands like ip, ss, ping, and traceroute remotely, and capture packet-level data with tcpdump when deeper analysis is needed. The hands-on examples show how to register outputs, make decisions with when conditionals, and fetch captures back for analysis. You will also learn safety considerations, such as limiting tcpdump filters and checking return codes before acting. By the end of this lesson you will be able to write playbooks that inspect interface state, verify listening ports, test external connectivity, and conditionally escalate diagnostics only when needed. This skillset reduces the need for manual logins, speeds triage across many hosts, and helps you avoid common mistakes like acting before collecting facts. Think about the last time you chased a networking issue by SSHing to one host; this chapter teaches you to do that reliably and at scale with Ansible.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives translate chapter outcomes into practical competencies you will use in the lab and on real systems. First, you will leverage Ansible facts to perform network introspection so you can quickly list interfaces, IPs, gateways, and other structured network resources without interactive logins. Second, you will run diagnostic commands remotely through Ansible—ip, ss, ping, and traceroute—and capture their outputs for later analysis. Each skill includes knowing how to register results and examine return codes. Third, you will author playbooks that perform automated connectivity checks and port scans across a host group, enabling consistent triage. Finally, you will learn to deploy tcpdump with appropriate filters via Ansible, collect captures, and understand the operational impact. Together these objectives help you move from manual troubleshooting to repeatable, auditable automation for network issues on RHEL hosts.

screens.title: Ansible Facts for Network Introspection
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible facts are the first and often most revealing source of information when troubleshooting network problems at scale. The setup module collects details about interfaces, addresses, MTU, and the primary IPv4 configuration. For network work, ansible_facts. interfaces gives you an indexed view of each interface and the data attached to it, while ansible_facts. default_ipv4 provides the host's active address and gateway. This saves time: rather than SSHing into dozens of servers to run ip addr, you can gather consistent structured data from all targeted hosts and compare configured values. A concrete example: if a host is unreachable from your monitoring system, examine ansible_facts. default_ipv4. gateway and the interface addresses to detect incorrect gateway assignment or missing IP. A common misconception is that facts are always current; facts reflect the state at collection time, so ensure you gather_facts when you need fresh data or re-run setup in playbooks that change interfaces. Takeaway: use facts to establish a reliable baseline, then follow up with targeted commands when facts suggest anomalies. Ansible Facts for Network Introspection means facts provide a consistent, machine-readable snapshot of network configuration so you can detect drift and surface incorrect interface or routing settings quickly.. In practical terms, gather structured network data automatically with ansible.builtin.setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept

Ansible Facts for Network Introspection

Gather structured network data automatically with ansible.builtin.setup
What facts give you
  • Interfaces list with addresses, MACs, and state via ansible_facts.interfaces.
  • Primary route and gateway in ansible_facts.default_ipv4.
  • Structured resources under ansible_facts.network_resources for deeper inspection.
Example
ansible_facts.default_ipv4: { address: 10.0.1.5, gateway: 10.0.1.1 }
Common misconception
Assuming facts always reflect real-time changes; re-run setup or gather_facts when you change interfaces in the same playbook.
Key Takeaway

Use Ansible facts as your baseline for network state before running higher-impact diagnostics or changes.

Inspecting facts: quick checklist
Interfaces
List names, IPs, and state
Default IPv4
Primary IP and gateway
Network Resources
Structured view for advanced checks
Freshness
Re-run setup when you need current state
Practical step
- name: Gather network facts ansible.builtin.setup: gather_subset: '!all', 'network'

screens.title: Diagnostic Commands via Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: A fundamental troubleshooting pattern is to execute the same command across many hosts and compare results. Ansible lets you run ip addr show to list addresses and interface states, ip route show to examine routing tables, ss -tulpn or netstat to find listening sockets, ping to test ICMP reachability, and traceroute to see the network path. Use ansible. builtin. command for simple invocations and ansible. builtin. shell when you need pipes or shell features; when you register the result, you capture stdout_lines and the return code for programmatic checks. For example, run ss -tulpn and register the output: you can then debug the stdout_lines to quickly see if a service listens on its expected port. A common error is using ping alone to conclude a service is down — ping tests reachability, not whether a process is listening. Another pitfall is assuming netstat output shows allowed traffic; firewall rules can still block connections. Takeaway: collect command output consistently, inspect rc and stdout_lines, and combine facts with command results for a complete picture. Diagnostic Commands via Ansible means commands show live state; combine them with facts and return-code checks to understand whether an issue is configuration, service, or network path related.. In practical terms, run ip, ss, ping, and traceroute remotely and interpret their output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison

Diagnostic Commands via Ansible

Run ip, ss, ping, and traceroute remotely and interpret their output
Quick command map
ip addr
List IPs and interface state.
ip route
Show routing table and default gateway.
ss -tulpn
Check listening ports and owning processes.
firewall-cmd
Inspect firewalld rules and zones.
Example
- name: Check open ports
  ansible.builtin.command: "ss -tulpn"
  register: open_ports_output
  changed_when: false

- name: Display open ports
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    var: open_ports_output.stdout_lines
Interpreting results
  • Always check rc to detect failures even when stdout exists.
  • Compare interface facts with ip addr output to detect drift.
  • Use traceroute when ping fails to locate hop-level failures.
Misconception
Passing ping does not guarantee an application is reachable; you must check service ports and firewall rules.
Key Takeaway

Run the same diagnostic commands via Ansible and register their output so you can programmatically compare and act on results across hosts.

screens.title: Registering Output and Using debug
screens.narratorSegment: Registering command output is how you make results usable in playbooks. When a task runs ansible. builtin. command or ansible. builtin. shell, add register: name to capture stdout, stderr, and rc. Use ansible. builtin. debug to inspect the captured stdout_lines during development so you understand the data structure. For example, register the result of ping and then check ping_result. rc to determine success. A concrete pattern is to run a command, register the result, and set changed_when: false for diagnostic tasks so playbooks remain read-only during checks. One important nuance: stdout_lines is an array of lines that is easy to iterate over for text searches, whereas stdout is the raw string. A common mistake is to try to use a registered variable before it is defined; ensure tasks that produce the variable run conditionally or use gather_facts to guarantee a sequence. Takeaway: treat register as your telemetry channel from remote hosts and use debug frequently while authoring playbooks so you can write robust when conditions against the actual output structure. Registering Output and Using debug means use register to capture diagnostics and inspect stdout_lines and rc values; then use those values in when clauses to control subsequent tasks.. In practical terms, capture stdout_lines and return codes for conditional decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow

Registering Output and Using debug

Capture stdout_lines and return codes for conditional decisions
Pattern
- name: Ping external IP
  ansible.builtin.command: "ping -c 3 8.8.8.8"
  register: ping_result
  ignore_errors: yes
  changed_when: false

- name: Debug ping output
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    var: ping_result.stdout_lines
Use ignore_errors when you expect failures and inspect rc to branch logic later.
Best practices
  • Set changed_when: false for diagnostic tasks to avoid false-positive changes.
  • Inspect rc to detect silent failures; rc != 0 usually indicates a problem.
  • Prefer stdout_lines when parsing output line-by-line.
Common mistake
Assuming registered output always exists; guard dependent tasks with when checks to avoid undefined-variable errors.
Key Takeaway

Register results, debug them while developing, and use rc and stdout_lines to drive reliable, conditional playbook flows.

screens.title: Conditional Execution with when
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional execution transforms diagnostics into targeted troubleshooting. Use when clauses to run tasks only if prior diagnostic tasks fail or return specific values. A common pattern is to register the result of ping and then run traceroute only when ping returns a non-zero rc. This reduces noise and avoids unnecessary captures. Concretely, run the ping task with register: ping_result and then a traceroute task with when: ping_result. rc!= 0. This ensures traceroute runs only when reachability is broken. A helpful contrast: some engineers run traceroute and tcpdump unconditionally; that can create large data and wasted effort. Remember to set changed_when and ignore_errors appropriately so diagnostic failures do not stop the entire playbook unexpectedly. Misconception to avoid: when operates on the registered result object, not on the raw stdout, so check the rc field or test string membership in stdout_lines. Takeaway: use when to make troubleshooting playbooks efficient, safe, and focused on hosts that actually need deeper inspection. Conditional Execution with when means use when with registered results so follow-up commands like traceroute run only when earlier checks, such as ping, indicate failure.. In practical terms, run follow-up diagnostics only when earlier checks indicate failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Targeted diagnostics
keyIdea.text: Use when with registered results so follow-up commands like traceroute run only when earlier checks, such as ping, indicate failure.

content.html:
Process Flow

Conditional Execution with when

Run follow-up diagnostics only when earlier checks indicate failure
Conditional example
- name: Test connectivity
  ansible.builtin.command: "ping -c 3 8.8.8.8"
  register: ping_google_output
  ignore_errors: yes
  changed_when: false

- name: Run traceroute if ping failed
  ansible.builtin.command: "traceroute 8.8.8.8"
  register: traceroute_output
  when: ping_google_output.rc != 0
  changed_when: false
Using rc in when avoids relying on fragile text parsing and ensures deterministic conditions.
Practical tips
  • Use changed_when and ignore_errors for diagnostics so playbooks remain readable and non-disruptive.
  • Prefer checking rc over parsing stdout when possible for stable conditions.
  • Guard later tasks that reference registered variables with when to avoid undefined errors.
Misconception
Assuming when will retry or recover; it only controls execution flow. You must handle retries or remediation explicitly.
Key Takeaway

Use when with registered rc values to run deeper diagnostics only where failures actually occur, keeping runs efficient and safe.

screens.title: Using tcpdump with Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Sometimes packet-level visibility is required, and tcpdump is the tool for that. With Ansible you can ensure tcpdump is installed, run it with a timeout and specific filter expression, and then fetch the resulting pcap for local analysis. A recommended pattern is to run tcpdump with timeout and a filter, for example capturing only traffic on port 80 for 10 seconds and writing to /tmp/capture. pcap; then use fetch to copy that file to your controller. Importantly, running tcpdump on production servers without filters or timeouts can fill disks and consume C P U. The chapter provides a safe example that uses creates to avoid duplicate captures and marks the task as changed_when: true because it writes a file. A common misconception is that tcpdump must be run indefinitely to capture useful data; focused, timeboxed, and well-filtered captures typically provide the evidence you need with far less impact. Takeaway: automate tcpdump via Ansible but always specify filters, time limits, and careful fetching to preserve production stability. Using tcpdump with Ansible means run tcpdump via ansible with filters and timeouts, then fetch the capture; avoid broad, long-running captures in production.. In practical terms, deploy, run filtered captures, and fetch pcap files safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe packet capture
keyIdea.text: Run tcpdump via Ansible with filters and timeouts, then fetch the capture; avoid broad, long-running captures in production.

content.html:
Definition

Using tcpdump with Ansible

Deploy, run filtered captures, and fetch pcap files safely
Safe capture example
- name: Ensure tcpdump is installed
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: tcpdump
    state: present

- name: Capture network traffic on eth0 for 10 seconds
  ansible.builtin.shell: "timeout 10 tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap 'port 80' || true"
  args:
    creates: /tmp/capture.pcap
  register: tcpdump_capture
  changed_when: true
Use creates to avoid repeated captures and timeout to limit duration.
Fetch pattern
- name: Fetch the captured pcap file
  ansible.builtin.fetch:
    src: /tmp/capture.pcap
    dest: /tmp/ansible_captures/{{ inventory_hostname }}/
    flat: yes
  when: tcpdump_capture.rc == 0
Safety note
Filtered, timeboxed captures reduce resource use. Avoid running tcpdump without explicit filters in busy production environments.
Key Takeaway

Automate packet captures safely: install tcpdump, run with filters/timeouts, and fetch captures only when successful.

screens.title: Example: Network Troubleshooting Playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Here we walk through a concise troubleshooting playbook that demonstrates many of the chapter patterns. The playbook starts by gathering facts, then prints the primary IP and gateway. It runs ss -tulpn to list listening ports and registers the output so you can debug it. The playbook then pings an external host with ignore_errors enabled and uses the ping result's return code to decide whether to run traceroute. This code pattern shows how to combine facts, command execution, register variables, and when conditionals into a coherent sequence. As a concrete walkthrough, note how changed_when is set to false for read-only checks and ignore_errors prevents the run from failing early so you can collect full diagnostics. A misconception to avoid is assuming registering output alone fixes the issue; these outputs inform your next steps, such as restarting services or adjusting firewall rules. content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Network Troubleshooting Playbook

A playbook that gathers facts, inspects ports, pings, and conditionally runs traceroute
---
- name: Network Troubleshooting Playbook
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes

  tasks:
    - name: Gather network facts (if not already gathered)
      ansible.builtin.setup
      when: ansible_facts is not defined or not ansible_facts.keys()

    - name: Display primary IP and gateway
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Primary IP: {{ ansible_facts.default_ipv4.address }}, Gateway: {{ ansible_facts.default_ipv4.gateway }}"

    - name: Check open ports on the server
      ansible.builtin.command: "ss -tulpn"
      register: open_ports_output
      changed_when: false

    - name: Display open ports
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: open_ports_output.stdout_lines

    - name: Test connectivity to an external host (e.g., google.com)
      ansible.builtin.command: "ping -c 3 google.com"
      register: ping_google_output
      ignore_errors: yes
      changed_when: false

    - name: Display ping results
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: ping_google_output.stdout_lines

    - name: Run traceroute if ping to external host failed
      ansible.builtin.command: "traceroute google.com"
      register: traceroute_output
      when: ping_google_output.rc != 0
      changed_when: false

    - name: Display traceroute results
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: traceroute_output.stdout_lines
      when: ping_google_output.rc != 0
Key Takeaway

This playbook pattern combines facts, registered outputs, and when conditionals to collect evidence and run follow-up diagnostics only when necessary.

screens.narratorSegment: When a service appears unreachable, the issue often lies in whether the process is listening or the firewall is blocking access. Use ss -tulpn to list TCP and UDP listeners and the owning process, which quickly verifies whether a service is bound to its expected port. Complement this with firewall-cmd --list-all or a zone-specific query to see which ports and services are allowed by firewalld. A practical example: if an HTTP service is not reachable, run ss -tulpn and look for a listener on port 80; if the process exists but connections still fail, check the public zone rules for that host to confirm port 80 is open. A common mistake is toggling services without checking firewall rules; that can mask the real problem. When automating these checks in Ansible, register both outputs and present them together so decision tasks have full context. Definition

Inspecting Ports and Firewall Rules

Check listener
- name: Check if SSH port (22) is listening
  ansible.builtin.command: "ss -ltn | grep ':22'"

  ansible.builtin.debug:

Use text checks for quick assertions, but prefer structured parsing where possible.
Check firewall
- name: Verify firewalld public zone rules
  ansible.builtin.command: "firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all"

  changed_when: false

A listening process guarantees connectivity; firewall policies can silently block traffic even when services are running.

Always validate both the listening socket and firewall configuration before assuming a service failure.

screens.title: Common Troubleshooting Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting at scale brings predictable pitfalls. First, many people act before they gather facts: making changes without collecting interface and routing facts can exacerbate problems. Second, ignoring return codes and relying only on stdout text can hide failures—check rc for deterministic behavior. Third, running heavy scans or long tcpdump captures on busy production servers can consume resources and create operational incidents. For example, running nmap or broad tcpdump filters without timeouts may trigger intrusion alerts or fill disks. Best practices address these mistakes: gather facts first, use register and debug to inspect outputs, prefer changed_when:false for diagnostic tasks, and design timeboxed and filtered captures. When using conditionals, check the registered object's rc or structured fields instead of brittle text parsing. A useful habit is to run diagnostic playbooks in read-only mode initially, collect artifacts, and then make changes only after evidence points to a specific fix. Takeaway: treat troubleshooting as evidence-driven and minimize your impact on production systems. Common Mistakes

Common Troubleshooting Mistakes and Best Practices

Avoid false assumptions, collect evidence first, and be mindful of production impact
Mistake: Act before facts
Change configuration without gathering facts and you may mask the real issue. Gather ansible_facts first.
Mistake: Ignore rc
Relying on stdout alone can miss command failures. Inspect the registered rc field to detect errors reliably.
Mistake: Unbounded captures
Running tcpdump without filters or timeouts risks resource exhaustion and triggers alerts. Timebox and filter captures.
Best practice checklist
  • Gather facts first, then run read-only diagnostics.
  • Register outputs, debug them, and use rc values in when conditions.
  • Limit the scope and duration of scans and captures in production.
Key Takeaway

Make troubleshooting repeatable and safe: collect evidence, use conditional logic, and limit operational impact.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to write playbooks that inspect interface state, verify listening ports, test external connectivity, and conditionally escalate diagnostics only when needed. Think about the last time you chased a networking issue by SSHing to one host; this chapter teaches you to do that reliably and at scale with Ansible.

Reflect on which tool you will use first when you need to determine whether an issue is a service misconfiguration, a firewall block, or a network path failure.
